analysis.one_liner: Bans most robocalls to homes and cell phones, unsolicited fax ads, and lets people sue telemarketers.
analysis.headline: The bill became law: it passed the Senate by voice vote on November 7, 1991, the House by voice vote on November 26, and the President signed it on December 20, 1991 as Public Law 102-243.
analysis.plain_summary: This law restricts telephone and fax marketing aimed at ordinary people. It bans calls made by automatic dialers or prerecorded voices to emergency lines, hospital rooms, pagers, and cell phones, and bars prerecorded calls to homes without the called party's consent. It outlaws unsolicited fax advertisements and requires faxes and recorded calls to identify who is sending them. It directs the FCC to write rules protecting people from unwanted sales calls, including possibly a national do-not-call list, and lets individuals and states sue violators for damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a home phone, fax machine, pager, or cell phone. The law cuts down on unwanted sales calls and junk faxes, protects numbers the called party pays for, and gives people the right to sue marketers who break the rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Home phone, fax, and cell phone users

how_it_helps.text: It bans calls made by automatic dialing systems or prerecorded voices to emergency lines at hospitals, fire departments, and law enforcement agencies, and to pagers, cell phones, and other numbers where the called party pays for the call [S3].
It bars prerecorded-voice calls to residential phone lines unless the called party consents, with specified exceptions [S3].
It prohibits sending unsolicited advertisements by fax machine and requires faxes and recorded messages to clearly identify the sender, the date and time sent, and a contact telephone number [S3].

It directs the FCC to write rules protecting residential subscribers from sales calls they object to, without charging subscribers extra, and allows a single national do-not-call database that telemarketers must buy access to [S3].
It authorizes private lawsuits with damages for violations, and lets states sue to stop violations affecting their residents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketers, call-center operations, and businesses that advertise by fax or robocall, which face new restrictions on whom they may call, what equipment they may use, and damages in private lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The House-passed version loosened the consent standard: the introduced bill required prior express written consent before a prerecorded call to a residence, while the House amendment required only consent of the called party, making the restriction easier for marketers to satisfy [S2] [S3].

The FCC may exempt categories of calls from the restrictions, including calls that are not commercial and commercial calls that do not adversely affect privacy rights or contain unsolicited advertisements, giving the agency room to narrow the rules [S3].

Compliance costs fall on telemarketers and on small businesses that used faxes or phone calls to reach customers, including limits on calling multi-line businesses where two or more lines would be engaged at once [S3].

Federal law preempts state rules: states cannot require a do-not-call system that excludes part of the national database, cannot sue a defendant already named in an FCC action, and their suits go to federal district court [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to ordinary people are real and durable: fewer robocalls and junk faxes, caller identification requirements, and a private right to sue that later underpinned the national do-not-call regime. The costs are borne by marketers and are modest relative to the nuisance removed. The main design weakness is that Congress gave the FCC broad authority to exempt calls and softened the consent requirement in the House, so the law's strength depends on how the FCC writes its rules.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the Senate by voice vote on November 7, 1991, the House took it up under a fast-track procedure and passed it by voice vote on November 26, the Senate accepted the House's changes the next day, and the President signed it on December 20, 1991.

narrative.text: Introduced July 11, 1991 by Senator Hollings and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which held hearings in its Communications Subcommittee on July 24 [S5].
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on July 30 and reported it on October 8, placing it on the Senate calendar [S5].
The Senate passed the bill with an amendment and an amendment to the title by voice vote on November 7, 1991 [S5].
The House passed the bill, as amended, by voice vote under suspension of the rules on November 26, 1991 [S5].
The Senate agreed to the House amendment by voice vote on November 27, and the President signed the bill on December 20, 1991, making it Public Law 102-243 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary telephone subscribers, whose homes, fax machines, and pay-per-call devices get statutory protection from automated marketing. Telemarketing operations lose some calling methods but remain in business under new FCC rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Phone and fax users, not telemarketers

sides.party_line_note: The record shows bipartisan support: cosponsors included 3 Democrats and 1 Republican, both chambers passed the bill by voice vote with no recorded opposition, and a Republican president signed it.

industries.note: The law restricts automated dialers, prerecorded calls to homes, and calls to cell phones and pagers, and opens marketers to private lawsuits with damages. It also entrenches the industry's role: the FCC was told to weigh telemarketers' needs in designing any national do-not-call database and to charge them fees for access rather than banning the practice outright.

industries.industry: Fax advertisers and fax machine manufacturers
industries.note: Unsolicited fax ads are banned and senders must identify themselves, costing advertisers a cheap marketing channel. Machine makers gain a mandate: faxes built a year after enactment must automatically stamp date, time, and sender information on each page.

A rider directs the FCC to pursue full-time signal status for existing daytime-only AM stations in larger communities that lack a local full-time station, a benefit to those specific licensees unrelated to the bill's consumer protections.

Residential customers get protection from unwanted sales calls without any added charge on their phone bills, and users of numbers they pay for (cell phones, pagers) are shielded from automated calls entirely.
